title: When Tool Outputs Become Commands
hook: Prompt injection into agents is really one confusion: the thing that suggests an action and the thing that authorizes it are treated as the same thing.
key_points: The paper's diagnosis: the risk comes from conflating action induction with execution authorization.
SARA separates them as distinct runtime roles — action provenance on one side, execution authority on the other.
A context-isolated Action Probe exposes action-inducing semantics in observations and records action-origin provenance across steps.
Tool calls are authorized only against the user objective plus audited evidence from prior authorized successes.
No-History-Promotion stops repeated appearances in history from laundering an action's origin into authority.
On AgentDojo and AgentDyn, attack success stays at or below 0.63% across four settings with competitive task utility.
content_html: An agent that browses, reads files, and calls APIs has to consume untrusted text. The danger arrives when a tool output stops being data and starts specifying an action — "now email this to that address" — because the agent has no principled way to say that a suggestion from a web page is not an instruction from its user. Guo and colleagues name this precisely: the risk comes from conflating action induction with execution authorization.
extra_html:
The design

SARA keeps the two as distinct runtime roles. On the observation side, a context-isolated Action Probe inspects tool output for action-inducing semantics and records action-origin provenance persistently across steps, as a review signal. On the execution side, an actual tool call is authorized only against the user's stated objective and audited evidence from previously authorized successful executions — checked for goal support, execution-chain support, and argument-level support.

The subtle piece is No-History-Promotion. Over a multi-step run, an injected suggestion that keeps reappearing starts to look like ordinary established context; the rule blocks that recurrence from converting an untrusted origin into execution authority.

Results

Across AgentDojo and AgentDyn, the authors report attack success rate held to at most 0.63% in four primary evaluation settings while maintaining competitive task utility, with consistent reductions across other agent backbones.

The conceptual takeaway outlives the specific system: agent security is largely a provenance and authority problem, of the kind operating systems have long solved by refusing to let data confer privilege.

related.title: Prompt Injection Defenses Fall Apart in Long Context
related.hook: Injection benchmarks are all short-context, which has been flattering the defenses. Stretch the input to tens of thousands of tokens and even naive attacks walk through state-of-the-art protections.

related.title: CamoDocs: Poisoning RAG Without Leaving Fingerprints
related.hook: Existing RAG poisoning attacks paste the target query into the malicious document, which is exactly what makes them easy to filter. CamoDocs hides the payload inside plausible benign text instead.

flashcards.prompt: What distinction does SARA argue agent frameworks collapse?
flashcards.back_html: Action induction (something suggests an action) versus execution authorization (something grants permission to perform it). Treating them as one lets untrusted tool output drive real side effects.

flashcards.prompt: What is the purpose of SARA's No-History-Promotion rule?

choices.text: To stop an action's untrusted origin being laundered into authority by recurring in history
To prevent the agent from reading its own earlier reasoning
To cap conversation length so injected text falls out of context

flashcards.explanation_html: Without it, an injected suggestion that appears repeatedly across steps starts to look like established context, and provenance is lost. The rule keeps origin attached to the action.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't agents just refuse to read untrusted tool output?
flashcards.back_html: Untrusted observations are the point — web pages, files, API responses are what the agent needs to complete open-ended tasks. The fix has to be about authority, not about avoiding the data.
